questions.q: In the Argand diagram, the points z with |z − 2 + i| = 3 form a circle. What are its centre and radius?
questions.x: |z − 2 + i| = |z − (2 − i)| is the distance of z from 2 − i, so the circle has centre (2, −1) and radius 3. Reading the signs straight off gives (−2, 1); 9 is the square of the radius.

questions.q: Which of these binary operations on R is commutative but NOT associative?
questions.x: (a + b)/2 = (b + a)/2, but (0 * 0) * 4 = 0 * 4 = 2 while 0 * (0 * 4) = 0 * 2 = 1. a + b + 1 is commutative and associative, a * b = a is associative but not commutative, and a − b is neither.

questions.q: What is the solution set of log₂(x − 3) < 2?
questions.x: The logarithm needs x − 3 > 0. The base 2 is greater than 1, so log₂(x − 3) < 2 means x − 3 < 2² = 4, i.e. x < 7. Together 3 < x < 7; forgetting the domain gives x < 7.

questions.q: At which point does the graph of y = 3·2ˣ − 1 cross the y-axis?
questions.x: At x = 0, 2⁰ = 1, so y = 3·1 − 1 = 2: the point (0, 2). Taking 2⁰ as 2 gives 5, and forgetting the −1 gives 3.

questions.q: lim(x→1) (x² + ax + b)/(x − 1) = 5. What are a and b?
questions.x: The denominator tends to 0, so the top must vanish at x = 1: 1 + a + b = 0. Then x² + ax + b = (x − 1)(x + 1 + a), and the limit is 2 + a = 5, so a = 3, b = −4. Check: (x² + 3x − 4)/(x − 1) = x + 4 → 5.

questions.q: A = [[2, −4], [1, −2]] and I is the 2 × 2 identity matrix. What is (I + A)³?
questions.x: A² = [[4 − 4, −8 + 8], [2 − 2, −4 + 4]] = O. Since I and A commute, (I + A)³ = I + 3A + 3A² + A³ = I + 3A. Direct check: both equal [[7, −12], [3, −5]].

questions.q: Dividing x³ + px² + qx − 6 by x − 2 gives quotient x² + x + 3 and remainder 0. What are p and q?
questions.x: (x − 2)(x² + x + 3) = x³ + x² + 3x − 2x² − 2x − 6 = x³ − x² + x − 6, so p = −1 and q = 1. Check with synthetic division by 2: coefficients 1, −1, 1, −6 give the row 1, 1, 3 and remainder 0.

questions.q: Which statement about the graph of y = 2x² − 3x + 5 is true?
o: It lies entirely above the x-axis
It touches the x-axis at exactly one point
It cuts the x-axis at two points
It lies entirely below the x-axis
questions.x: The discriminant is 9 − 40 = −31 < 0, so there are no real roots, and with a = 2 > 0 the parabola opens upward. So it lies entirely above the x-axis. Check: the minimum is 5 − 9/8 = 31/8 > 0.

questions.q: If (x² + 1)/(x(x² + 2)) = A/x + (Bx + C)/(x² + 2), what is the value of A?
questions.x: x² + 1 = A(x² + 2) + (Bx + C)x. Put x = 0: 1 = 2A, so A = 1/2. Then B = 1/2 and C = 0. Forgetting to divide by the 2 from x² + 2 gives 1.

questions.q: How many terms of the A.P. 20, 17, 14, … are positive?
questions.x: aₙ = 20 − 3(n − 1) = 23 − 3n > 0 gives n < 23/3 ≈ 7.7, so n = 1 to 7. Check: a₇ = 2 and a₈ = −1. Rounding 7.7 up gives 8.

questions.q: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the two numbers differ by exactly 2?
questions.x: The pairs are (1, 3), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 6) and the same four reversed: 8 of the 36 outcomes, so 8/36 = 2/9. Forgetting the reversed pairs gives 4/36 = 1/9.

questions.q: In the expansion of (1 + x)ⁿ, three consecutive coefficients are 6, 15 and 20. What is n?
questions.x: Let the coefficients be ⁿCᵣ₋₁, ⁿCᵣ, ⁿCᵣ₊₁. Then (n − r + 1)/r = 15/6 gives 2n + 2 = 7r, and (n − r)/(r + 1) = 20/15 gives 3n − 4 = 7r. So 2n + 2 = 3n − 4 and n = 6; indeed ⁶C₁, ⁶C₂, ⁶C₃ = 6, 15, 20.

questions.q: The 3rd term in the expansion of (2 + x)⁵ is:
questions.x: The 3rd term has r = 2: ⁵C₂ · 2³ · x² = 10 × 8 x² = 80x². Taking r = 3 for the 3rd term gives the wrong power, and forgetting the factor 2³ gives 10x².

questions.q: Given that sin 18° cos 36° = 1/4, what is the value of sin 47° + sin 61° − sin 11° − sin 25°?
questions.x: sin 47° − sin 25° = 2 cos 36° sin 11° and sin 61° − sin 11° = 2 cos 36° sin 25°. Their sum is 2 cos 36°(sin 11° + sin 25°) = 2 cos 36° × 2 sin 18° cos 7° = 4 sin 18° cos 36° cos 7° = cos 7°.

questions.q: Given sin 2θ = 24/25 with 0 < θ < π/4, what is tan θ?
questions.x: sin 2θ = 2t/(1 + t²) with t = tan θ, so 24t² − 50t + 24 = 0, i.e. 12t² − 25t + 12 = 0, giving t = 3/4 or 4/3. Since θ < π/4, tan θ < 1, so tan θ = 3/4. 4/3 belongs to θ between π/4 and π/2, and 24/7 is tan 2θ.

questions.q: What is the range of y = sin²x − sin x + 1?
questions.x: With t = sin x ∈ [−1, 1], y = (t − 1/2)² + 3/4. The least value 3/4 is at t = 1/2, inside the interval; the greatest is at t = −1: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. Checking only t = ±1 gives [1, 3] and misses the vertex.

questions.q: A triangle has escribed radii r₁ = 2, r₂ = 3 and r₃ = 6. What is its area?
questions.x: 1/r = 1/r₁ + 1/r₂ + 1/r₃ = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 1, so r = 1. Then Δ² = r r₁ r₂ r₃ = 36 and Δ = 6. (It is the 3-4-5 triangle.) 36 forgets the square root, and 1 is r.

questions.q: tan⁻¹(3/4) equals:
questions.x: If tan θ = 3/4 with θ acute, the right triangle has sides 3, 4 and hypotenuse 5, so sin θ = 3/5 and θ = sin⁻¹(3/5). sin⁻¹(4/5) is the other acute angle, tan⁻¹(4/3).

questions.q: The general solution of sin⁴θ − cos⁴θ = 1/2 is (n ∈ Z):
questions.x: sin⁴θ − cos⁴θ = (sin²θ − cos²θ)(sin²θ + cos²θ) = −cos 2θ, so cos 2θ = −1/2, 2θ = 2nπ ± 2π/3, θ = nπ ± π/3. Check π/3: 9/16 − 1/16 = 1/2. Missing the minus sign gives cos 2θ = 1/2 and nπ ± π/6.

questions.q: A curve is given by x = sin t, y = cos 2t. What is dy/dx in terms of x?
questions.x: dy/dx = (−2 sin 2t)/(cos t) = (−4 sin t cos t)/cos t = −4 sin t = −4x. Check: y = 1 − 2 sin²t = 1 − 2x², so dy/dx = −4x. −2 sin 2t is only dy/dt.

questions.q: If f(x) = tan x, what is the value of f′(π/4)?
questions.x: f′(x) = sec²x and sec(π/4) = √2, so f′(π/4) = (√2)² = 2. The value 1 is tan(π/4) itself, and √2 forgets to square.

questions.q: ∫ x³/(x² − 1) dx, for x > 1, equals:
questions.x: The fraction is improper, so divide first: x³/(x² − 1) = x + x/(x² − 1). Then ∫x dx = x²/2 and ∫x/(x² − 1) dx = ½ ln(x² − 1), giving x²/2 + ½ ln(x² − 1) + C.

questions.q: The region under one arch of y = sin x, from x = 0 to x = π, is rotated about the x-axis. The volume of the solid is:
questions.x: V = π∫₀^π sin²x dx = π∫₀^π ½(1 − cos 2x) dx = π × π/2 = π²/2. Using y instead of y² gives π∫sin x dx = 2π.

questions.q: A town's population grows at a rate proportional to its size. It is 2000 now and 3000 after one year. What will it be after two years?
questions.x: P = 2000e^(kt) with e^k = 3/2, so P(2) = 2000 × (3/2)² = 4500. Adding 1000 each year (linear growth) gives 4000.

questions.q: An equilateral triangle has one vertex at the origin and the opposite side on the line x + y = 2. What is the length of its side?
questions.x: The height is the distance from O to the line: 2/√2 = √2. For an equilateral triangle h = (√3/2)s, so s = 2√2/√3 = 2√6/3. √2 is the height, not the side.

questions.q: The equation ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0 (b ≠ 0) represents the lines y = m₁x and y = m₂x. What are m₁ + m₂ and m₁m₂?
questions.x: Put y = mx: bm² + 2hm + a = 0, whose roots are m₁ and m₂, so the sum is −2h/b and the product a/b. Check with x² − 3xy + 2y² = 0: the lines y = x and y = x/2 have sum 3/2 and product 1/2.

questions.q: A satellite moves on an ellipse with the Earth's centre at one focus. Its least and greatest distances from the Earth's centre are 2 and 8 units. What is the eccentricity of the orbit?
questions.x: Least distance a − c = 2 and greatest a + c = 8 give a = 5 and c = 3, so e = c/a = 3/5. 1/4 is just the ratio of the two distances.

questions.q: Which equation represents a real circle?
questions.x: A circle needs equal x² and y² coefficients and g² + f² − c > 0. For the first, 1 + 4 − 1 = 4 > 0 (centre (1, −2), radius 2). The last has 1 + 4 − 6 < 0, so it has no real points.

questions.q: a and b are non-zero vectors that are not parallel, and (x − 2)a + (y + 1)b = 3a − 2b. What are x and y?
questions.x: Because a and b are not parallel, the coefficients can be compared: x − 2 = 3 and y + 1 = −2, so x = 5 and y = −3.

questions.q: To find 1/3 without dividing, Newton–Raphson is applied to f(x) = 1/x − 3. Which iteration results?
questions.x: f′(x) = −1/x², so xₙ₊₁ = xₙ − (1/xₙ − 3)/(−1/xₙ²) = xₙ + xₙ − 3xₙ² = xₙ(2 − 3xₙ). Check: x = 1/3 gives (1/3)(2 − 1) = 1/3, a fixed point.

questions.q: A mass of 0.00340 kg is converted to grams. Correctly written, it is:
questions.x: 0.00340 kg = 3.40 g. Changing units does not change the number of significant figures: 0.00340 has three (the leading zeros do not count, the trailing zero does), so 3.40 g. Dropping the trailing zero gives 3.4 g.

questions.q: A 100 N weight hangs at rest from two strings. One string makes 60° with the horizontal and the other 30° with the horizontal, on opposite sides (sin 30° = 0.5, sin 60° = √3/2). The tension in the string at 60° to the horizontal is:
questions.x: Horizontally T₁ cos 60° = T₂ cos 30°, so T₂ = T₁/√3; vertically T₁ sin 60° + T₂ sin 30° = 100, giving T₁(√3/2 + 1/(2√3)) = 100, so T₁ = 50√3 N and T₂ = 50 N. The strings are perpendicular, so T₁ = 100 sin 60° confirms it. 50 N is the tension in the other string.

questions.q: A block of weight 60 N rests on a smooth plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. It is held at rest by a horizontal force F (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = √3/2). The normal reaction of the plane on the block is:
questions.x: Along the plane: F cos 30° = 60 sin 30°, so F = 60/√3 = 20√3 N. Perpendicular: N = 60 cos 30° + F sin 30° = 30√3 + 10√3 = 40√3 N (check: N = W/cos 30° = 120/√3 = 40√3 N). 30√3 N forgets the push of F into the plane; 20√3 N is F itself.

questions.q: A projectile launched from level ground at angle θ with speed v has range R. Ignoring air resistance, if it is launched at the same angle with speed 2v, its range becomes:
questions.x: R = v² sin 2θ/g, so R ∝ v²: doubling the speed makes the range 4R. Taking R proportional to v gives 2R.

questions.q: Ignoring air resistance, a ball thrown from level ground with a fixed speed travels the greatest horizontal distance when it is thrown at an angle above the horizontal of:
questions.x: Range R = v² sin 2θ/g is greatest when sin 2θ = 1, that is θ = 45°. At 90° the range is zero; 30° and 60° give equal but smaller ranges.

questions.q: A 2 kg ball is thrown vertically upward and rises 5 m. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the work done on the ball by gravity during the rise is:
questions.x: Gravity (20 N) acts downward while the displacement is 5 m upward, so W = 20 × 5 × cos 180° = −100 J. Ignoring the direction gives +100 J; using the mass instead of the weight gives −10 J.

questions.q: A wheel of radius 0.5 m turns at 600 rev min⁻¹. The centripetal acceleration of a point on its rim is:
questions.x: 600 rev min⁻¹ = 10 rev s⁻¹, so ω = 20π rad s⁻¹ and a = rω² = 0.5 × 400π² = 200π² m s⁻² (about 2000 m s⁻²). Forgetting to square ω gives 10π; using 10 rev s⁻¹ as ω gives 50 m s⁻²; leaving out r gives 400π².

questions.q: The SI unit of angular acceleration is:
questions.x: Angular acceleration = change in angular velocity (rad s⁻¹) ÷ time (s), so its unit is rad s⁻². rad s⁻¹ is the unit of angular velocity, the usual mix-up.

questions.q: A 0.2 kg mass on a spring performs SHM with amplitude 0.1 m. Its maximum speed is 1 m s⁻¹. The spring constant is:
questions.x: Energy: ½kx₀² = ½mv_max², so k = mv²/x₀² = 0.2 × 1/0.01 = 20 N m⁻¹ (check: ω = v/x₀ = 10 rad s⁻¹ and k = mω² = 20 N m⁻¹). Not squaring the amplitude gives 2 N m⁻¹; 10 is ω.

questions.q: A particle in SHM has a period of 1.2 s and starts from its mean position. The least time it takes to reach a displacement equal to half its amplitude is:
questions.x: x = x₀ sin ωt with x = x₀/2 gives sin ωt = ½, so ωt = π/6 and t = T/12 = 0.1 s. Assuming constant speed (half of T/4) gives 0.15 s; 0.3 s is the time to reach the full amplitude.

questions.q: A pipe 0.85 m long is open at both ends. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. Its fundamental frequency is:
questions.x: An open pipe has antinodes at both ends, so L = λ/2 for the fundamental: λ = 1.7 m and f = 340/1.7 = 200 Hz. The closed-pipe formula v/4L gives 100 Hz; 600 Hz is the third harmonic.

questions.q: Newton's rings are seen in reflected light of wavelength 600 nm, with a dark spot at the centre. Counting the central spot as the zeroth dark ring, what is the thickness of the air film at the 5th dark ring?
questions.x: With the extra phase change of π on reflection, dark rings occur where 2t = mλ, so t = 5 × 600/2 = 1500 nm = 1.5 μm. Each dark ring adds λ/2 = 300 nm of film, and 5 × 300 nm agrees. Forgetting the factor 2 gives 3.0 μm.

questions.q: A Young's double-slit apparatus has slits 0.4 mm apart and a screen 1.0 m away. It is lit by light containing wavelengths 600 nm and 400 nm together. Apart from the centre, what is the nearest distance from the central fringe at which bright fringes of both colours fall together?
questions.x: The bright fringes coincide where m₁ × 600 = m₂ × 400; the smallest is 2 × 600 = 3 × 400 = 1200 nm. Then y = 1200 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.0/(0.4 × 10⁻³) = 3.0 mm. Check: the fringe spacings are 1.5 mm and 1.0 mm, whose first common multiple is 3.0 mm. 1.5 mm is only the 600 nm spacing.

questions.q: The resolving power of an optical instrument describes its ability to:
o: Show two close objects as separate
Collect more light from a faint object
questions.x: Resolving power is the ability to distinguish two nearby points or objects as separate; it is set by the minimum angle of resolution. Making things look larger is magnifying power, a different idea.

questions.q: A petrol engine has an efficiency of 25% and delivers a power of 15 kW. How much heat does it reject to the surroundings each second?
questions.x: Heat input per second = 15/0.25 = 60 kJ; heat rejected = 60 − 15 = 45 kJ each second. 60 kJ is the heat taken in, not rejected.

questions.q: A closed surface encloses charges of +3 nC and −1 nC. A charge of +5 nC lies just outside it. The total electric flux through the closed surface is:
questions.x: By Gauss's law the flux depends only on the net charge inside: (3 − 1) nC = 2 nC, so Φ = (2 nC)/ε₀. The outside charge sends as much flux in as out. Including it gives 7 nC.

questions.q: Compared with the gravitational force between two electrons at the same separation, the electrostatic force between them is:
o: Far larger, by a factor of about 10⁴²
Larger by a factor of about 10
questions.x: ke²/(Gmₑ²) ≈ (9 × 10⁹ × 2.6 × 10⁻³⁸)/(6.7 × 10⁻¹¹ × 8.3 × 10⁻⁶¹) ≈ 4 × 10⁴². Both follow an inverse-square law, so the ratio does not depend on distance; gravity is far weaker.

questions.q: A uniform wire of resistance R draws a current I from a fixed p.d. V. The wire is cut into four equal pieces, which are then connected in parallel across the same p.d. V. The current drawn from the supply is now:
questions.x: Each piece has resistance R/4; four of them in parallel give (R/4)/4 = R/16. With the same V, the current becomes 16I. Stopping after cutting (R/4) gives 4I.

questions.q: A 3 Ω and a 6 Ω resistor are connected in parallel, and this pair is in series with a 2 Ω resistor. The current in the 3 Ω resistor is 2 A. The p.d. across the 2 Ω resistor is:
questions.x: The p.d. across the parallel pair is 2 × 3 = 6 V, so the 6 Ω resistor carries 1 A. The total current is 3 A, and the p.d. across the 2 Ω resistor is 3 × 2 = 6 V. Using only the 2 A in the 3 Ω resistor gives 4 V.

questions.q: Which physical quantity has the SI unit N m A⁻¹?
questions.x: 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹, and flux Φ = BA has unit T m² = N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ × m² = N m A⁻¹, which is the weber. Flux density itself is N A⁻¹ m⁻¹.

questions.q: The total force F = qE + q(v × B) on a charge moving through both an electric and a magnetic field is called the:
questions.x: The combined electric and magnetic force on a moving charge is the Lorentz force. The Coulomb force is only the electric part qE; emf is not a force at all.

questions.q: When the current in a coil changes by 2 A in 0.1 s, an emf of 20 V is induced in it. The energy stored in the coil when it carries a steady current of 3 A is:
questions.x: L = ε/(ΔI/Δt) = 20/(2/0.1) = 1 H, and U = ½LI² = ½ × 1 × 9 = 4.5 J. Dropping the ½ gives 9 J; forgetting to square the current gives 1.5 J.

questions.q: Two alternating voltages of the same frequency are v₁ = V₀ sin ωt and v₂ = V₀ cos ωt. Which statement is correct?
questions.x: cos ωt = sin(ωt + 90°), so v₂ reaches each value a quarter cycle earlier than v₁: v₂ leads by 90°. For example, v₂ is at its peak at t = 0, when v₁ is still zero.

questions.q: For the same increase in pressure, the fractional decrease in volume is greatest for a gas and least for a solid. Comparing the bulk moduli, this means that:
o: Solids have the largest bulk modulus and gases the smallest
Gases have the largest bulk modulus and solids the smallest
All three have the same bulk modulus
Liquids have the largest bulk modulus
questions.x: Bulk modulus K = Δp/(ΔV/V), so a smaller fractional volume change for the same Δp means a larger K. Solids are hardest to compress (largest K) and gases easiest (smallest K). Mixing up K with compressibility, its reciprocal, reverses the order.

questions.q: The small current that flows through a reverse-biased p-n junction is carried mainly by:
o: Majority carriers: holes in the p-region and electrons in the n-region
Minority carriers: holes in the n-region and electrons in the p-region
The fixed ions in the depletion region
questions.x: Reverse bias stops the majority carriers, but the junction field sweeps across the few thermally produced minority carriers, giving a tiny reverse current. Fixed ions cannot move, so they carry no current.

questions.q: A particle moves so fast that its relativistic mass is twice its rest mass m₀. Its kinetic energy is:
questions.x: Kinetic energy = total energy − rest energy = mc² − m₀c² = 2m₀c² − m₀c² = m₀c². Taking the total energy 2m₀c² as the kinetic energy is the usual slip; ½m₀v² does not apply at such speeds.

questions.q: The Compton effect, in which X-ray photons lose energy when scattered by electrons, is strong evidence that photons:
o: Carry momentum and collide like particles
questions.x: Compton explained the wavelength shift by treating the photon as a particle with momentum h/λ colliding elastically with an electron, conserving energy and momentum. Photons have zero rest mass and travel at c.

questions.q: In an ordinary lamp, excited atoms return to lower levels by spontaneous emission. The photons given out in spontaneous emission have:
o: The same phase and the same direction
The same phase but random directions
questions.x: Spontaneous emission happens at random, without any triggering photon, so the photons go out in all directions with unrelated phases, giving incoherent light. Same phase and same direction is the mark of stimulated emission.

questions.q: In a solid-state (semiconductor) detector, radiation is detected when it enters a reverse-biased p-n junction and:
o: Produces electron-hole pairs, which give a small pulse of current
Makes the junction forward biased permanently
questions.x: Radiation passing through the depletion region creates electron-hole pairs; the reverse-bias field sweeps them out as a pulse of current, whose size depends on the energy deposited. Visible droplet tracks belong to a cloud chamber.

questions.q: The antiproton is the antiparticle of the proton. Its quark content and charge are:
questions.x: An antiparticle is made of the antiquarks of the particle's quarks, with opposite charges: ū (−⅔e), ū (−⅔e), d̄ (+⅓e) give −⅔ − ⅔ + ⅓ = −1e. ū d̄ d̄ is the antineutron, with charge 0.

questions.q: A sample of neon gives peaks in its mass spectrum at m/e 20 and 22 only, with relative heights 9 : 1. The relative atomic mass of this neon is:
questions.x: Weighted mean = (20 × 9 + 22 × 1)/10 = 202/10 = 20.2. Swapping the abundances gives 21.8, and taking a plain average of 20 and 22 gives 21.0.

questions.q: For a compound X, (concentration in ether) ÷ (concentration in water) = 2 at equilibrium. 9.0 g of X is dissolved in 100 cm³ of water and extracted with two successive 50 cm³ portions of ether. The total mass of X extracted into the ether is:
questions.x: With 50 cm³ ether: (mₑ/50) ÷ (m_w/100) = 2, so mₑ = m_w and each portion takes half of what is left: 4.5 g, then 2.25 g, total 6.75 g. One 100 cm³ portion would take only 6.00 g, and stopping after the first portion gives 4.50 g.

questions.q: In a vessel at room temperature, gas molecules do not settle at the bottom under gravity. According to the kinetic molecular theory, this is because:
o: They are in rapid random motion and their kinetic energy is very large compared with the effect of gravity on them
The walls of the vessel attract them
questions.x: Gas molecules move very fast in random directions and keep colliding, so gravity has only a tiny effect over the height of a vessel. Strong repulsion is not a postulate, and molecules do have mass.

questions.q: In a cubic unit cell, atoms of P occupy all the corners and atoms of Q occupy the centres of all the faces. The simplest formula of the compound is:
questions.x: Corners: 8 × ⅛ = 1 P. Face centres: 6 × ½ = 3 Q. So the formula is PQ₃. Counting each face atom as a whole (6 Q to 1 P) gives PQ₆.

questions.q: How many subshells are present in the shell with n = 3?
questions.x: l takes values 0 to n − 1, i.e. 0, 1, 2 for n = 3: the 3s, 3p and 3d subshells. A 3f subshell would need l = 3, which is not allowed for n = 3; nine is the number of orbitals.

questions.q: The mass of a proton is approximately how many times the mass of an electron?
questions.x: m(proton)/m(electron) = 1.6726 × 10⁻²⁷ / 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ ≈ 1836. The electron is the much lighter particle, so 1/1836 is the ratio the other way round.

questions.q: Which of these molecules has a bond order of 2.5 according to molecular orbital theory?
questions.x: NO has 11 valence electrons: 8 bonding and 3 antibonding (σ*2s² and one π*2p), so bond order = ½(8 − 3) = 2.5. N₂ and CO (10 valence electrons) have bond order 3, and O₂ (12) has 2.

questions.q: A reaction is carried out inside a tightly stoppered, perfectly insulated flask that lets neither heat nor matter pass through its walls. The contents of the flask form:
questions.x: An isolated system exchanges neither energy nor matter with its surroundings. A closed system exchanges energy but not matter; a stoppered but uninsulated flask would be closed, which makes that option tempting.

questions.q: At a certain temperature, Kc for a reaction is about 10³⁰. This tells us that at equilibrium:
o: The mixture is almost all reactants
The reaction reaches equilibrium very quickly
Reactants and products are present in nearly equal amounts
The mixture is almost all products, so the reaction goes practically to completion
questions.x: Kc is products over reactants, so a huge value means the products dominate the equilibrium mixture. K says nothing about how fast equilibrium is reached; that depends on the rate, which is the tempting confusion.

questions.q: The contact process is used to manufacture:
questions.x: In the contact process SO₂ is oxidised to SO₃ over a catalyst, and the SO₃ is turned into H₂SO₄. Ammonia is made by the Haber process, the usual mix-up.

questions.q: In the reaction HCO₃⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → CO₃²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l), the hydrogencarbonate ion acts as:
o: A Brønsted–Lowry base, because it accepts a proton
A Lewis base, because it donates an electron pair to OH⁻
A Brønsted–Lowry acid, because it donates a proton to OH⁻
An Arrhenius base, because it produces OH⁻
questions.x: HCO₃⁻ loses H⁺ to become CO₃²⁻, and OH⁻ gains it to become H₂O, so HCO₃⁻ is the proton donor (acid) here. HCO₃⁻ can act as a base towards stronger acids, which is why that option is tempting, but not in this reaction.

questions.q: Which change is a hydrolysis rather than a hydration?
questions.x: In hydrolysis a water molecule is split: here the acetate ion takes H⁺ from water and leaves OH⁻. In hydration whole water molecules simply attach to ions or form a hydrate, as in the other three changes.

questions.q: A standard cell is made from a nickel electrode, E°(Ni²⁺/Ni) = −0.25 V, and a copper electrode, E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V. What is the emf of the cell, and which way do electrons flow in the external wire?
questions.x: Nickel, with the more negative E°, is the anode and is oxidised; electrons leave it and flow to the copper cathode. E°cell = 0.34 − (−0.25) = 0.59 V. Subtracting the numbers without their signs gives 0.09 V.

questions.q: The rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction rises as the temperature is raised to about 37–40 °C but falls sharply at higher temperatures. The fall is mainly because:
o: The activation energy rises at higher temperatures
The molecules collide less often at higher temperatures
The enzyme, a protein, is denatured and loses its active shape
questions.x: Enzymes are proteins; heat breaks the weak bonds that hold their shape, so the active site is lost and catalysis stops. Collisions actually become more frequent at higher temperature.

questions.q: In the liquid state, which chloride does NOT conduct electricity?
questions.x: SiCl₄ is a simple covalent molecular liquid with no ions, so it does not conduct. Molten NaCl, MgCl₂ and CaCl₂ are ionic and conduct because their ions are free to move.

questions.q: Lime mortar, a paste of slaked lime, sand and water, slowly hardens in air. The main reaction is:
questions.x: Slaked lime in the mortar absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and turns into hard calcium carbonate as the water evaporates. CaO + H₂O is the earlier slaking step, and the gypsum reaction belongs to plaster, not lime mortar.

questions.q: Borax is used as a flux in soldering and brazing metals. When molten, borax cleans the metal surface because it:
o: Dissolves the metal oxide film, forming fusible metaborates
Reduces the metal oxide film back to the metal
Covers the metal with a hard layer of boron nitride
Lowers the melting point of the metal itself
questions.x: Fused borax gives NaBO₂ and B₂O₃, and B₂O₃ combines with basic metal oxides to form low-melting metaborates, so the oxide layer is removed and the solder can wet the metal (the same chemistry as the borax bead). Thinking borax acts as a reducing agent is the usual slip.

questions.q: In the Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, the catalyst used is:
questions.x: Ammonia is made over finely divided iron promoted with small amounts of K₂O and Al₂O₃. V₂O₅ is the contact process catalyst and platinum gauze is used in the Ostwald process, so those are the usual mix-ups.

questions.q: The formula usually given for bleaching powder is:
questions.x: Bleaching powder, made from chlorine and dry slaked lime, is written Ca(OCl)Cl (calcium chloride hypochlorite). NaOCl is liquid household bleach and Ca(ClO₃)₂ is a chlorate, so NaOCl is the tempting mix-up.

questions.q: When KMnO₄ acts as an oxidising agent in neutral or weakly alkaline solution, the manganese product and the number of electrons gained per MnO₄⁻ ion are:
questions.x: In neutral or weakly alkaline solution MnO₄⁻ is reduced to a brown precipitate of MnO₂, Mn going from +7 to +4, a gain of 3 electrons. Mn²⁺ with 5 electrons is the change in acidic solution, the most tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂COCl is:
questions.x: –COCl is an acid (acyl) chloride group; with three carbons including the C=O carbon, the name is propanoyl chloride. Propyl chloride is CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl, which has no carbonyl group.

questions.q: Ethyne is mixed with excess hydrogen and passed over heated nickel. The final product is:
questions.x: With excess H₂ both π bonds are hydrogenated: HC≡CH + 2H₂ → CH₃CH₃. Ethene is only the intermediate; stopping there needs a poisoned catalyst and one mole of H₂.

questions.q: 1,3-Dimethylbenzene is heated with excess hot alkaline KMnO₄ and the mixture is then acidified. The organic product is:
questions.x: KMnO₄ oxidises every alkyl side chain on a benzene ring to –COOH while leaving the ring intact; with excess oxidant both methyl groups are oxidised. 3-Methylbenzoic acid assumes only one side chain reacts.

questions.q: 4.6 g of ethanol is converted completely into bromoethane with PBr₃: 3C₂H₅OH + PBr₃ → 3C₂H₅Br + H₃PO₃. What mass of bromoethane is formed? (C₂H₅OH = 46, Br = 80)
questions.x: 4.6/46 = 0.10 mol ethanol gives 0.10 mol C₂H₅Br (ratio 3:3). M(C₂H₅Br) = 24 + 5 + 80 = 109, so 0.10 × 109 = 10.9 g. Dividing by 3 (reading the ratio as 3:1) gives 3.6 g; multiplying by 3 gives 32.7 g.

questions.q: Glucose is fermented by yeast: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. What mass of ethanol can be obtained from 90 g of glucose? (C₆H₁₂O₆ = 180, C₂H₅OH = 46 g mol⁻¹)
questions.x: 90/180 = 0.5 mol glucose gives 2 × 0.5 = 1.0 mol ethanol = 46 g. Ignoring the 1:2 ratio gives 23 g; 44 g is the mass of CO₂ formed, not ethanol.

questions.q: 0.10 mol of but-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃, undergoes ozonolysis (zinc and water work-up). What mass of ethanal forms? (CH₃CHO = 44 g mol⁻¹)
questions.x: Each but-2-ene gives two CH₃CHO, so 0.20 mol × 44 = 8.8 g. Forgetting that both halves give ethanal gives 4.4 g; 5.8 g uses the molar mass of propanone.

questions.q: In the zwitterion of alanine, ⁺H₃NCH(CH₃)COO⁻, the group that donates a proton when a base such as NaOH is added is:
questions.x: In the zwitterion the acidic proton is on nitrogen: ⁺H₃N– + OH⁻ → H₂N– + H₂O, giving the anion. The –COO⁻ group is the base, which accepts a proton from an acid; picking it mixes up the two roles.

questions.q: Methylamine, CH₃NH₂, is treated with nitrous acid (NaNO₂ and dilute HCl) at room temperature. The main organic product and the gas given off are:
questions.x: A primary aliphatic amine forms an unstable diazonium ion that at once loses N₂, and water gives the alcohol: CH₃NH₂ + HNO₂ → CH₃OH + N₂ + H₂O. The bubbles of N₂ are a test for primary amines; ammonia is not formed.

questions.q: Complete hydrolysis of maltose gives:
questions.x: Maltose is two α-glucose units joined by a 1,4-glycosidic link, so hydrolysis gives only glucose. Glucose and fructose come from sucrose, and glucose and galactose from lactose; these are the usual mix-ups.

questions.q: Ammonium nitrate fertiliser is manufactured by:
o: Heating ammonia with carbon dioxide under pressure
Treating rock phosphate with nitric acid
Passing nitrogen through hot calcium carbide
questions.x: NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃; the solution is concentrated and made into granules. Ammonia with CO₂ under pressure is the urea process, the usual mix-up.

questions.q: For the instruction ADD, during which step of the instruction cycle does the ALU actually add the two numbers?
questions.x: The instruction is first fetched from memory, then decoded so the control unit knows it means ADD; the adding happens in the execute step. In the decode step the operation is only identified, not carried out.

questions.q: Taking 1 TB = 1,024 GB, a 1 TB hard disk holds how many gigabytes?
questions.x: Each step up from GB to TB is a factor of 1,024, so 1 TB = 1,024 GB. 1,000,000 is close to 1,024 × 1,024, the number of megabytes in 1 TB, not gigabytes.

questions.q: During the fetch step, the address in the memory address register goes to memory, and the instruction comes back to the memory data register. Which buses are used for these two movements, in that order?
questions.x: The address travels from the MAR to memory on the address bus, and the instruction read from that location travels back to the MDR on the data bus. The control bus only carries signals such as 'memory read', not the address or the instruction.

questions.q: In data communication, the path along which the message travels from the sender to the receiver, such as a cable or radio waves, is called the:
questions.x: The medium is the physical path the signal travels through, wired or wireless. The protocol is the set of rules both sides follow, not the path itself.

questions.q: A WAN that joins offices in different countries usually carries data over:
o: One short coaxial cable in a single building
Leased telecom lines, undersea cables and satellite links
A single hub in the head office
questions.x: Distant sites are linked through telecom providers' long-distance lines, cables and satellites. Infrared only works over a few metres in line of sight, so it cannot join offices in different countries.

questions.q: The physical arrangement in which the computers, cables and other devices of a network are connected is called the network's:
questions.x: Topology is the layout of the connections, such as bus, star, ring or mesh. A protocol is the set of rules for communication, not the layout.

questions.q: Copyright, patents and trademarks are all forms of:
questions.x: Intellectual property rights protect creations of the mind; copyright, patents and trademarks are its main forms. They are legal rights, not crimes or security methods.

questions.q: Which statement about open-source software is correct?
o: It is always in the public domain, with no copyright at all
Nobody is allowed to change its source code
Its authors still hold the copyright, and its licence sets the conditions for sharing it
It must always be paid for before it is used
questions.x: Open-source programs are copyrighted works released under a licence that allows studying, changing and sharing under stated conditions. Public domain work, by contrast, has no copyright holder.

questions.q: The Internet of Things needs a huge number of devices, each with its own address on the network. How does IPv6 help?
o: It makes devices work without any network
It provides far more addresses than IPv4
It allows only one device per home
questions.x: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses instead of IPv4's 32-bit ones, giving vastly more addresses for billions of devices. It does not remove the need for a network.

questions.q: Hospitals keep patients' histories, test results and prescriptions on computers so that any authorised doctor can view them. These are called:
questions.x: Electronic medical (health) records store patient information digitally for authorised staff. An expert system gives advice from stored knowledge; it is not a record store.

questions.q: When a file is double-clicked, how does Windows decide which program opens it?
o: By its extension and the program linked to that extension
By the size of the file
By the date the file was made
By the folder the file is kept in
questions.x: Windows links each file extension, such as .docx or .xlsx, with a program (file association), and opens the file with that program. Size, date and folder do not decide this.

questions.q: In a word processor, font sizes such as 12 and 14 are measured in:
questions.x: Font size is given in points, where 72 points make one inch. Bytes measure data size, not text size.

questions.q: In Book(AccessionNo, ISBN, Title, Author), every physical copy has its own AccessionNo, and the library keeps several copies of many titles, which share one ISBN. Which column can be the primary key?
questions.x: Only AccessionNo is different for every copy, so it can identify each row. ISBN is repeated for copies of the same title, so it is not unique in this table.

questions.q: A copy of the master file is kept on a separate disk so that the data can be restored if the original is damaged. What is this copy called?
questions.x: A backup file is a copy kept for restoring data after loss or damage. A transaction file holds recent changes that are used to update the master file.

questions.q: The Marks field has a Validation Rule. Which property holds the message, such as "Marks must be 0 to 100", that Access shows when an entry breaks the rule?
questions.x: Validation Text is the message displayed when the Validation Rule is broken. Input Mask controls the pattern of typing, and Format controls how values are displayed.

questions.q:
Table Book(BookID, Title, Subject, Price) holds these rows: (1, Algebra, Maths, 450), (2, Optics, Physics, 600), (3, Calculus, Maths, 700), (4, Atoms, Chemistry, 350), (5, Mechanics, Physics, 500), (6, Geometry, Maths, 400).
What does this query return?
```
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Book WHERE Subject = 'Maths' AND Price > 450;
```
questions.x: The Maths books cost 450, 700 and 400; only 700 is greater than 450, so the count is 1. Algebra at 450 is not counted because > does not include 450.

questions.q: Which is a correct difference between `#define N 10` and `const int n = 10;`?
o: N can be changed later by an assignment; n cannot
N is replaced by 10 before compiling and has no data type; n is an int whose value cannot change
N is stored in memory as an int; n is replaced by 10 before compiling
There is no difference except the spelling of the names
questions.x: A macro is plain text substitution done by the preprocessor, so N has no type and no memory. The const declaration makes a real int variable that the compiler will not let the program change.
The variables are set in order: a = 3, then b = 3 + 2 = 5, then c = 3 × 5 = 15. 9 would come from using a * a.

questions.q: Which `while` loop prints the same output as `for (i = 0; i < 5; i++) printf("%d ", i);`?
questions.x: A for loop does its update after the body, so the while version must print first and then increase i, starting at 0 with the test i < 5: it prints 0 1 2 3 4. Increasing i before printing gives 1 2 3 4 5, and <= 5 adds an extra 5.

questions.q: In the function definition `int max(int a, int b) { ... }`, the first line `int max(int a, int b)` is called the:
questions.x: The header (declarator) gives the return type, the name and the parameters, and the body in braces follows it. A prototype looks similar but stands alone and ends with a semicolon.

o: Adds the contents of `old.txt` to the end of what `new.txt` already holds
Moves the text out of `old.txt`, leaving it empty
Prints the contents of `old.txt` on the screen
questions.x: Each character read from old.txt with fgetc is written to new.txt with fputc until EOF, so new.txt becomes a copy. new.txt is opened with "w", which starts it empty, so nothing is added to old contents; old.txt is only read, so it is unchanged.
i takes the values 5, 3, 1; the next value -1 fails the test i > 0, so the loop stops before printing it.

questions.q: For a library management system, which of these is a functional requirement?
o: The system must show search results within 2 seconds
The system must let a member reserve a book that is currently issued
The system must run on computers with 4 GB of RAM
The system must be available 24 hours a day
questions.x: A functional requirement says what the system must do (a service such as reserving a book). Speed, hardware and availability describe how well or where it works, so they are non-functional requirements.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
print("a" + str(1 + 2) + "b" * 2)
```
questions.x: `1 + 2` is 3, `str` makes it "3", and `"b" * 2` is "bb"; joining gives a3bb. No error occurs because the number is converted to a string before `+`.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
print("2026".isdigit(), "20.26".isdigit())
```
questions.x: `isdigit()` is True only when every character of the string is a digit. "2026" qualifies; "20.26" contains a full stop, so it gives False even though it looks like a number.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
def rev(s):
    r = ""
    for ch in s:
        r = ch + r
    return r
print(rev("abc") + rev("12"))
```
questions.x: Each character is put in front of r, so the string comes out reversed: rev("abc") is "cba" and rev("12") is "21". Joined in order: cba21. cba12 forgets that the second call also reverses.

questions.q: Why is adding a new first element quicker in a linked list than at the start of an array-style list?
o: Only a few links change; no existing element has to be shifted
A linked list keeps its elements sorted
A linked list stores all its elements in one block of memory
A linked list can be searched with binary search
questions.x: The new node just points to the old first node and becomes the head. In an array every existing element must move one place to make room. It is the array, not the linked list, that uses one block of memory.

questions.q: p: "It is raining." q: "The ground is wet." Which sentence is the converse of p → q?
o: If it is not raining, then the ground is not wet.
If the ground is not wet, then it is not raining.
It is raining and the ground is wet.
If the ground is wet, then it is raining.
questions.x: The converse swaps the two parts: q → p. "If the ground is not wet, then it is not raining" is ¬q → ¬p, the contrapositive.

questions.q: Coins of Rs 1, Rs 3 and Rs 4 are available in any number. A greedy method pays Rs 6 by always taking the largest coin that does not exceed the amount still to pay. How many coins does it use?
questions.x: Greedy first takes 4 (2 left), then cannot take 3 or 4, so takes 1 and 1: three coins. Greedy does not look ahead, so it misses the better answer 3 + 3; there is no Rs 2 coin for 4 + 2.

questions.q: A model scores 99% accuracy on the data it was trained on but only 60% on new test data. What does this most likely show?
o: It needs to be tested on its training data only
It has overfitted: it fits the training data too closely and does not generalise
The test data must be wrong, so the test should be ignored
It is the best possible model, since training accuracy matters most
questions.x: A model that does very well on its training data but much worse on unseen data has learnt the training examples rather than the general pattern: overfitting. Evaluation on unseen test data is exactly what reveals this.

questions.q: Which statement best describes what the passage is about?
o: An aunt's anger at a niece who wasted cloth
The history of block printing in the town of Hala
How wooden blocks are carved into patterns of leaves
A girl's struggle with a craft and her discovery that skill means doing it again and again
questions.x: The narrator spoils cloth, finally makes a clean print and understands that "a whole cloth of them would be skill". The aunt shows no anger: she "said nothing" and handed the block back.

questions.q: According to the passage, what happened when the narrator pressed a pale patch a second time?
o: The block cracked under the extra pressure
The dye ran off the edges of the cloth
The colour became too dark to use
The outline was doubled and the cloth was spoiled
questions.x: Pressing again, she "doubled the outline and spoiled the whole length of cloth". Nothing is said about the block cracking.

questions.q: The aunt's habit of saying nothing and handing back the block suggests that she:
o: had lost interest in teaching her niece
thought the narrator would never learn
wanted her to try a different pattern
expected mistakes as a normal part of learning
questions.x: She "simply laid out another strip" each time, and when a good print came she set the next task, "Now do it four hundred more times". Losing interest is wrong: she kept supplying cloth for a whole week.

questions.q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "whole" most nearly means:
questions.x: The leaves sat on the cloth "sharp and dark and whole", unlike the earlier prints that were "blurred at one edge and pale at the other". "Healthy" is an old sense of the word, used of people.

questions.q: What does the narrator's laughter at the end of the passage most likely show?
o: Good-humoured acceptance that one success is only a beginning
Pleasure that her aunt had praised her at last
Relief that her training was now over
Scorn for her aunt's refusal to praise her
questions.x: She laughs "but I understood": "One good print was luck; a whole cloth of them would be skill". Relief is wrong, since the aunt has just given her four hundred more prints to make.

questions.q: The writer's main aim in the passage is to:
o: warn that lift cables often snap in tall buildings
explain how to escape from a lift stuck between floors
reassure readers that lifts are very safe by explaining how they are designed
describe how electricity is used to power lifts
questions.x: The passage answers the fear "What if the cable snaps?" by describing the several ropes, the governor and a brake that "fails safe". It says the fear "has been out of date for well over a century", not that cables often snap.

questions.q: What does the governor do if the car begins to drop faster than a set limit?
o: It cuts off the electricity to the lift
It attaches an extra steel rope to the car
It lowers the car slowly to the ground floor
It makes clamps grip the rails along which the car runs
questions.x: "The governor trips a pair of clamps fitted to the car. These grip the steel rails along which it runs". Nothing is said about cutting the power; the brake works without it.

questions.q: If the power failed at the same moment as the ropes, the passage suggests the car would:
o: fall freely, because the brake runs on electricity
still be stopped, because the clamps need no electricity
keep moving until the power came back
be held up by the governor's own motor
questions.x: The governor stops a car that drops too fast, and the clamps "need no electricity to work": "A power cut therefore does not disable the brake." Joining these, the car would still be stopped.

questions.q: As used in the third paragraph, the phrase "fails safe" means that the design:
o: breaks down more often than other designs
never needs to be checked or repaired
ends up in a safe state when something goes wrong
can fail only in places where no one is hurt
questions.x: The clamps "snap shut when released", so a fault such as "A power cut" leaves the car held where it is: failure leads to safety. Breaking down more often reads "fails" literally and ignores "safe".

questions.q: What role does the first paragraph play in the passage?
o: It describes an accident that the passage goes on to explain
It gives the history of the first lifts
It admits the writer's own fear of lifts
It presents a common fear that the rest of the passage answers
questions.x: It raises the question "What if the cable snaps?", and the following paragraphs explain why this fear is "out of date". No accident is described, and the unease belongs to "Many people", not the writer.
